chapter_title: Working with Redis Strings and Basic Commands
chapter_summary:
In the previous chapter, we touched upon the fundamental `SET` and `GET` commands for Redis Strings. Now, let's dive deeper into the capabilities of this versatile data type. While "string" might sound simple, Redis strings are binary-safe, meaning they can hold any kind of data, from plain text to JPEG images or serialized objects (like JSON). They can be up to 512 MB in size, making them suitable for storing substantial pieces of information. Beyond just storing and retrieving, Redis provides a rich set of commands to interact with string values in powerful ways.

One of the most critical features for caching and session management is the ability to set an **expiration time** for a key. This ensures that data doesn't live in Redis indefinitely, preventing stale data and managing memory usage. The `EXPIRE` command sets a timeout on a key in seconds.
```redis
SET user:session:12345 "user_data_serialized"
EXPIRE user:session:12345 3600  # Key will expire in 1 hour (3600 seconds)
```
You can check the remaining time-to-live (TTL) for a key using the `TTL` command. It returns the remaining time in seconds, or -2 if the key doesn't exist, or -1 if the key exists but has no associated expire.
```redis
TTL user:session:12345
```
For more granular control, `PEXPIRE` sets the expiration in milliseconds, and `PTTL` retrieves it in milliseconds. If you want to remove the expiration from a key, use `PERSIST`. This is incredibly useful for temporary data like user sessions, one-time tokens, or cache entries that should only be valid for a limited period. Forgetting to set expirations can lead to Redis memory filling up with old, unused data, impacting performance and potentially causing out-of-memory errors.

Redis also offers powerful atomic operations for numeric string values. The `INCR` and `DECR` commands are used to atomically increment or decrement a number stored as a string. "Atomic" means these operations are guaranteed to complete entirely without interruption, even if multiple clients try to modify the same key simultaneously. This prevents race conditions, which are common pitfalls in concurrent programming.
```redis
SET page:views:homepage 0
INCR page:views:homepage   # Returns 1
INCR page:views:homepage   # Returns 2
DECR page:views:homepage   # Returns 1
INCRBY page:views:homepage 10 # Returns 11 (increments by a specific amount)
DECRBY page:views:homepage 5  # Returns 6 (decrements by a specific amount)
```
These commands are perfect for implementing counters (like website page views, likes on a post), rate limiting (incrementing a counter for each request within a time window), or generating unique IDs. A common mistake here is trying to `INCR` or `DECR` a key that holds a non-numeric string, which will result in an error. Always ensure the value is an integer or can be converted to one.

When you need to interact with multiple keys at once, `MSET` and `MGET` come to the rescue, allowing you to set or get multiple key-value pairs in a single command. This reduces network round-trip times, significantly improving performance for bulk operations.
```redis
MSET user:1:name "Alice" user:1:email "alice@example.com" user:2:name "Bob"
MGET user:1:name user:1:email user:2:name user:3:name
```
The `MGET` command will return a list of values in the order of the keys requested. If a key doesn't exist, its corresponding value in the list will be `(nil)`. These commands are invaluable for fetching multiple related pieces of data in a single go, such as all the attributes for a user profile, or updating several configuration settings.

Finally, Redis strings offer commands for partial manipulation. `GETRANGE` retrieves a substring of a string, specified by start and end offsets (0-indexed).
```redis
SET mylongstring "This is a very long string."
GETRANGE mylongstring 0 3   # Returns "This"
GETRANGE mylongstring 10 14 # Returns "very "
```
`SETRANGE` overwrites a part of a string starting at a specified offset. If the string is shorter than the offset, it's padded with null bytes.
```redis
SET greeting "Hello World"
SETRANGE greeting 6 "Redis" # greeting becomes "Hello Redis"
GET greeting
```
These commands might seem niche, but they are incredibly useful for tasks like updating specific fields within a large serialized JSON string (though Hashes are often better for this), or manipulating binary data chunks. For example, if you're storing a bitmap or a part of a file, `SETRANGE` can update a specific segment without reading and rewriting the entire value.

By mastering these string commands, you unlock a vast array of possibilities for leveraging Redis in your applications, from building robust caching layers to implementing real-time features with atomic counters.

narration.text: In this lesson we'll go beyond simple SET and GET and explore the full power of Redis strings. You will learn that strings are binary-safe, can store up to large values, and support specialized commands for time-based expiry, atomic numeric updates, bulk operations, and partial updates. These features make strings useful for caching, session storage, counters, and compact binary blobs. We'll practice commands such as EXPIRE, TTL, PERSIST for lifetime control, INCR/DECR/INCRBY/DECRBY for safe counters, MSET/MGET to reduce network round trips, and GETRANGE/SETRANGE for precise substring edits. Throughout, I will show command-line examples and explain common mistakes, like incrementing non-numeric strings or forgetting to set expirations. By the end you will be able to pick the right string command for caching and counters and know how to inspect TTLs to avoid stale data. Keep an eye out for small gotchas—like the difference between seconds and milliseconds—and think about how these primitives map to your application's sessions and metrics.

screens.title: Binary-safe Strings and Size Limits
screens.subtitle: What Redis strings can store and when to use them

narration.text: Redis strings are deceptively powerful. When we say "string" in Redis we mean a binary-safe sequence of bytes. That means you can store plain text, JSON, serialized objects, images, or other binary data without worrying about character encoding. Redis supports large string values — up to hundreds of megabytes — which makes strings suitable for many payloads, though you should consider memory and network costs when storing very large blobs. A concrete example: storing a serialized user session as a JSON string works well for small sessions, and storing a compressed image chunk is fine because Redis treats it as a sequence of bytes. A common misconception is assuming Redis strings are only for human-readable text; they are not. Another mistake is overusing massive strings when a more structured approach, like hashes or external object storage plus a key reference, is more appropriate. Key takeaway: use strings for compact or binary payloads and counters, but consider data structure alternatives when you need field-level updates or when individual values grow very large. Ask yourself: will I often update parts of this value, or do I need atomic numeric operations? That choice guides whether to use strings or a higher-level structure.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Redis strings are binary-safe byte sequences and suitable for both text and binary payloads—choose them when you need compact, whole-value storage.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Binary-safe Strings
Definition

Binary-safe strings

Strings are byte arrays. They can contain text, serialized JSON, or binary data. Use them when you need whole-value reads and writes.

Concrete examples
Serialized session
Store a JSON session token as a single string and set an expiry for automatic cleanup.
Binary blob
Store compressed image chunks as bytes when you need fast in-memory access.
When not to use
If you need frequent partial updates to fields, prefer hashes over large serialized strings.
Key takeaway
Strings are versatile but choose structure when you need field-level operations.
Terminal demo
SET user:session:12345 "{\"user_id\":123,\"name\":\"Alice\"}"
GET user:session:12345
# Store a binary chunk (illustrative bytes shown as base64)
SET file:chunk:1 "\xFF\xD8\xFF..."
GET file:chunk:1
Explanation & common misconception
  • Although called "strings", Redis treats values as raw bytes. This is why binary data works without encoding changes.
  • Storing very large values is supported, but network and memory trade-offs matter — consider external storage for huge files.
  • For frequent partial updates, hashes or separate keys often produce simpler and smaller updates than repeated string rewrites.

screens.title: EXPIRE, TTL, and PERSIST
screens.subtitle: Control key lifetimes to manage cache and session data

narration.text: Managing key lifetime is essential when Redis holds temporary data. The EXPIRE command sets a timeout in seconds on a key. TTL returns the remaining time in seconds, or special sentinel values if the key doesn't exist or has no expiry. PERSIST removes any expiry, making a key permanent again. A concrete example: set a serialized session and EXPIRE it for one hour so stale sessions vanish automatically. Check TTL immediately to confirm — it should report a value less than or equal to the expiry you set. Common mistakes include forgetting to set expiries for session keys, which can cause memory to fill with stale data, and misinterpreting TTL results: TTL returns -2 when the key does not exist and -1 when it exists but has no expiry. Always verify TTL after setting expiry during debugging. Key takeaway: use EXPIRE and PERSIST intentionally to control memory and ensure temporary data behaves predictably. EXPIRE, TTL, and PERSIST means set expirations for temporary data; use ttl to inspect and persist to cancel expiry when needed.. In practical terms, control key lifetimes to manage cache and session data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lifetime management
keyIdea.text: Set expirations for temporary data; use TTL to inspect and PERSIST to cancel expiry when needed.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › EXPIRE, TTL, PERSIST
Commands
# Set a session and expire in 3600 seconds
SET user:session:12345 "user_data_serialized"
EXPIRE user:session:12345 3600

# Inspect remaining time
TTL user:session:12345   # returns remaining seconds

# Remove expiry
PERSIST user:session:12345
TTL user:session:12345   # returns -1 when no expiry
Why it matters

Expired keys free memory automatically and keep your cache and session store tidy. Use PERSIST only when you intentionally want a key to outlive its original TTL.

Diagnostics & pitfalls
  • TTL returns -2 if the key does not exist. Verify the key exists before interpreting negative TTL values.
  • TTL returns -1 if the key exists but has no expiration. This often reveals when you forgot to set EXPIRE.
  • Setting expirations in milliseconds uses PEXPIRE and PTTL. Choose seconds or milliseconds based on required precision.
Key Takeaway

Always set expirations for temporary data and use TTL to confirm; PERSIST can cancel expiry when you want permanence.

narration.text: Sometimes you need more precision than seconds. PEXPIRE sets a timeout in milliseconds and PTTL returns the remaining milliseconds. This is especially useful for short-lived tokens, fine-grained rate limiting, or synchronized time windows where second-granularity is too coarse. A concrete example: when implementing a per-user short lock that should last 250 milliseconds, use PEXPIRE to ensure the lock is released precisely. A common misconception is treating PEXPIRE as redundant when EXPIRE seems sufficient; in fact, millisecond precision can avoid race windows in some algorithms. Another pitfall is assuming TTL and PTTL values are exact to the millisecond at all times—Redis stores expirations precisely but network delays and slight clock differences mean you should design systems tolerant to small timing variances. Key takeaway: choose PEXPIRE/PTTL when you require fine-grained expirations, and use PERSIST to remove a millisecond expiry if you need to make the key permanent again. PEXPIRE and PTTL — Millisecond precision means pexpire and pttl provide millisecond precision for timeouts—useful for short-lived tokens and precise rate-limiting windows.. In practical terms, when sub-second precision matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Precision expiry
keyIdea.text: PEXPIRE and PTTL provide millisecond precision for timeouts—useful for short-lived tokens and precise rate-limiting windows.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › PEXPIRE / PTTL
Millisecond timeout
# Set a very short lock for 250 milliseconds
SET resource:lock "locked"
PEXPIRE resource:lock 250
PTTL resource:lock   # returns remaining milliseconds
Use PEXPIRE when you need sub-second control. PTTL mirrors TTL but returns milliseconds. This helps reduce tiny race windows in short-lived operations like ephemeral locks or micro-batching windows.
Pitfalls & practical notes
  • Network latency can affect perceived expiry; the value stored is precise but your client may observe small delays.
  • When combining with INCR counters or rate limiting, ensure your token-bucket windows account for boundary cases.
  • Use PERSIST to cancel millisecond expirations when a key must be promoted to permanent storage.
Check your understanding
When would you prefer PEXPIRE over EXPIRE? Think short locks and precise rate windows where second precision is too coarse.

screens.title: INCR, DECR, INCRBY, DECRBY
screens.subtitle: Atomic numeric updates for counters and IDs

narration.text: Atomic numeric operations are a core strength of Redis strings. INCR and DECR increment or decrement a numeric value stored as a string by one, and variants INCRBY and DECRBY change the value by a specified amount. Atomic means these operations complete fully without interruption, so concurrent clients cannot produce inconsistent counters. A practical example: initialize a page view counter to zero, then call INCR for each view; regardless of concurrent requests, the final count will be accurate. A common error is attempting to increment a non-numeric string, which results in an error. Always ensure the key holds an integer or can be interpreted as one; if not, reset or handle the exception. Use these commands for page view counts, like counters, or generating simple incremental IDs. Key takeaway: prefer INCR family operations for concurrency-safe increments rather than read-modify-write sequences that are vulnerable to race conditions. INCR, DECR, INCRBY, DECRBY means use incr/decr and their by variants to safely update numeric strings under concurrency without race conditions.. In practical terms, atomic numeric updates for counters and ids. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Atomic counters
keyIdea.text: Use INCR/DECR and their BY variants to safely update numeric strings under concurrency without race conditions.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › INCR / DECR family
Atomic numeric ops
# Initialize counter
SET page:views:/products/1 0

# Simulate views
INCR page:views:/products/1
INCR page:views:/products/1
DECR page:views:/products/1
INCRBY page:views:/products/1 10
DECRBY page:views:/products/1 5

# Read final value
GET page:views:/products/1
Example use
Page view counter: INCR is perfect because it avoids race conditions from concurrent requests.
Common mistake
Trying to INCR a non-numeric value will error. Validate or initialize values as integers before incrementing.
Checklist
  • Ensure the key is an integer or initialize it with SET key 0.
  • Use BY variants for batched increments to reduce repeat calls.
  • Prefer INCR family to read-modify-write sequences to avoid race conditions.
Key Takeaway

Use atomic commands for counters so multiple clients cannot produce incorrect values.

screens.title: Counter use case and rate limiting
screens.subtitle: Implementing safe counters and a basic rate limit window

narration.text: Let's apply atomic increments to a real use case: building a page view counter and a simple rate limiter. Begin by initializing the counter to zero. For each page request call INCR — this is safe even under concurrent requests. For rate limiting, you can use a key per user and EXPIRE it after your window duration. Example pattern: increment a counter and set an expiry of 60 seconds when the key is first created. If the count exceeds your threshold within the window, deny the request. The trick is to ensure the expiry is set only when the key is new; using INCR followed by EXPIRE can race if multiple clients run these operations separately. A common pattern is to use INCR and then a separate EXPIRE only when the returned value is one, which indicates the key was created by this client. Misconceptions include assuming INCR alone handles expiry; it does not. Key takeaway: combine atomic INCR with expiry to implement reliable counters and simple rate-limit windows without locks. Counter use case and rate limiting means use incr + conditional expire to build accurate rate limits and counters that expire automatically after a time window.. In practical terms, implementing safe counters and a basic rate limit window. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Use INCR + conditional EXPIRE to build accurate rate limits and counters that expire automatically after a time window.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Counter patterns
Terminal pattern
# Initialize
SET page:views:/products/1 0

# On each request
new = INCR page:views:/products/1
# For rate limiting per-user
count = INCR user:123:requests
if count == 1:
  EXPIRE user:123:requests 60  # set 60s window

# Check and enforce
if GET user:123:requests > 100:
  reject_request()
Note: The conditional EXPIRE after INCR ensures only the client creating the key sets the expiry. This reduces race conditions where multiple clients set different expiries or overwrite each other.
Example scenario
Imagine tracking requests per IP for an API. Each request INCRs an IP-specific key. The first INCR triggers an expiry of 60 seconds, creating a sliding window. Exceeding a threshold can trigger throttling. This design avoids distributed locks and relies on atomic increments plus expirations.
Gotcha
If you set EXPIRE unconditionally after INCR, multiple clients can race and overwrite the TTL; using the returned value to conditionally EXPIRE avoids this.

screens.title: SET/GET vs MSET/MGET
screens.subtitle: Reducing network round trips with bulk commands

narration.text: When you need to read or write multiple keys, network latency can dominate performance. SET and GET operate on single keys; MSET and MGET let you handle many keys in one command. A clear example: fetching three attributes for a product with separate GETs creates three round trips. Using MGET returns all values in one reply, improving latency and simplifying client code. MSET similarly sets multiple key-value pairs atomically in a single call. A common misconception is that MGET returns a dictionary — it returns a list of values in the same order as the requested keys, and missing keys produce nulls. This ordering is important when mapping results back to fields. Use MSET/MGET for related attributes fetched together, like product name, price, and category, to minimize network overhead. Key takeaway: when operations touch many keys at once, prefer multi-key commands for efficiency and simpler client-side logic. SET/GET vs MSET/MGET means use mset/mget to reduce network round trips and fetch related values atomically in one call; handle nulls for missing keys.. In practical terms, reducing network round trips with bulk commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bulk efficiency
keyIdea.text: Use MSET/MGET to reduce network round trips and fetch related values atomically in one call; handle nulls for missing keys.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › SET/GET vs MSET/MGET
Single vs Bulk
# Single requests (3 round trips)
GET product:1:name
GET product:1:price
GET product:1:category

# Bulk request (1 round trip)
MGET product:1:name product:1:price product:1:category
Mapping results
MGET returns values in the same order as keys. If a key is missing, its slot is nil. Map by position, not by key name.
When to use
  • Use MGET when you need several related values at once to reduce latency.
  • Use MSET when setting multiple keys together, for atomic multi-key writes.
  • For independent keys that are rarely fetched together, single GETs may be fine.
Key Takeaway

Bundle related reads and writes with MGET and MSET to reduce network trips and simplify client logic; handle nils for missing keys.

screens.title: GETRANGE and SETRANGE
screens.subtitle: Extracting and overwriting parts of a string

narration.text: GETRANGE and SETRANGE let you operate on slices of a string without replacing the whole value. GETRANGE returns a substring defined by start and end offsets (0-indexed). SETRANGE overwrites starting at a byte offset; if the string is shorter than the offset, Redis pads it with null bytes up to that position. A concrete example: GETRANGE mylongstring 0 3 returns the first four bytes, while SETRANGE greeting 6 "Redis" changes "Hello World" into "Hello Redis" by overwriting at offset six. These operations are handy for editing serialised blobs when you need to change a small field, but remember that using structured types like hashes may be cleaner when you need many field-level updates. A common misconception is thinking SETRANGE shifts the remaining bytes — it does not; it replaces bytes at offsets and may extend the string. Key takeaway: use GETRANGE/SETRANGE for targeted edits on large strings, and choose hashes when you need frequent, readable field updates. GETRANGE and SETRANGE means getrange extracts offsets; setrange overwrites bytes at an offset and may pad with nulls if extending the value.. In practical terms, extracting and overwriting parts of a string. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Partial edits
keyIdea.text: GETRANGE extracts offsets; SETRANGE overwrites bytes at an offset and may pad with nulls if extending the value.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › GETRANGE / SETRANGE
Examples
SET mylongstring "This is a very long string."
GETRANGE mylongstring 0 3    # -> "This"
GETRANGE mylongstring 10 14  # -> "very "

SET greeting "Hello World"
SETRANGE greeting 6 "Redis"
GET greeting                   # -> "Hello Redis"
Notice SETRANGE overwrites bytes starting at an offset. If the target offset is larger than the current length, Redis pads the value with null bytes. This behavior is important when manipulating binary chunks.
When to prefer hashes
If you find yourself routinely replacing different fields inside a serialized value, a hash structure that stores each field separately may be easier to work with than repeated SETRANGE edits.
Check your understanding
Does SETRANGE insert or replace? It replaces at the offset and may extend the string with padding, it does not shift bytes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Hands-on Activity
Starter commands
# 1. Initialize page view counter
SET page:views:/products/1 0

# 2. Simulate 5 page views
INCR page:views:/products/1
INCR page:views:/products/1
INCR page:views:/products/1
INCR page:views:/products/1
INCR page:views:/products/1

# 3. Retrieve current page view count
GET page:views:/products/1

# 4. Set a user session with expiration
SET user:session:abc "{\"user_id\": 123, \"username\": \"testuser\", \"login_time\": \"2023-10-27T10:00:00Z\"}"
EXPIRE user:session:abc 60

# 5. Check TTL
TTL user:session:abc
# Wait 10 seconds then TTL user:session:abc

# 6. Use MSET for product details
MSET product:1:name "Laptop Pro" product:1:price "1200.00" product:1:category "Electronics"

# 7. MGET product details
MGET product:1:name product:1:price product:1:category product:2:name
Expected observations & checks
  • After five INCR calls the GET should return "5". This proves atomic increments worked.
  • TTL should return a value near 60 immediately, and about 50 after waiting 10 seconds, confirming expiry counts down.
  • MGET returns values in the requested order; product:2:name returns nil when missing, indicating (nil) slots in the response.
Common gotcha
Remember to escape quotes in JSON strings inside your shell, or use single quotes outside the JSON to avoid syntax errors in the terminal.

narration.text: A few final practical reminders. Use MSET and MGET to reduce network round trips when reading or writing related keys. For partial updates use GETRANGE and SETRANGE, but prefer hashes if you require frequent field-level changes. Test TTLs and expirations when debugging temporary data; remember TTL returns -2 for missing keys and -1 for keys with no expiry. Finally, always validate numeric values before calling INCR or DECR to avoid errors. These concise rules help you make correct design choices when integrating Redis strings into your applications.
